AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING WHICH WILL ALSO INCLUDE
  A MEETING OF THE CITY COUNCIL ACTING AS
  THE SUCCESSOR AGENCY TO THE ACIA AND THE HOUSING AUTHORITY, AND
  THE HOUSING AUTHORITY TUESDAY, DECEMBER 12, 2023 5:00 PM  —

  410 AVALON CANYON ROAD
  THIS VIRTUAL MEETING IS HELD PURSUANT TO AB 361
  AGENDA

  In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this
  meeting, please contact the City Clerk’s Office (310) 510-0220. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting will
  enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35. 102-
  35.104 ADA Title II). All public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the public
  inspection at the time the records are distributed to all, or a majority of all, members of the City Council. Such
  records shall be available at City Hall located at 410 Avalon Canyon Rd.

Due to social distancing recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State of
California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA) and the County of Los
Angeles, and pursuant to findings made under AS 361, the CITY OF AVALON’S CITY COUNCIL
SHALL GENERALLY BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC REMOTELY. The general public may
attend the meeting in the Council Chambers however must adhere to social distancing
requirements. The public is encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes
while practicing social distancing.

Council Chambers are open to the general public. Once the Council Chambers reach maximum
occupancy (as determined by the Fire Chief), the general public may participate in Oral
Communication and address the City Council on an agenda item in person by waiting in the City
Hall Court Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time at the appropriate time. No one will be
admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. Additionally,
the general public may participate in Oral Communication and address the City Council on an
agenda items by providing comments via Zoom or by sending comments to
askcityofavalon .com.

  For the public’s convenience, but not participation, the meeting can be viewed:
  On local cable: Catalina Broadband Solutions channel 3
  Streaming Online: www.cityofavalon.com/meetings
  *Streaming on Facebook Live: www.facebook.com/CityOfAvalonOfficial
  Streaming on YouTube: https:/lwww.youtube.com/CityofAvalonCA

FOR REMOTE PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
1) Join the Meeting via Phone Conference (Voice Only):
  Phone Number: (669) 444-9171,
  Meeting ID: 812 4963 9798
  Passcode: 637481

When you would like to comment during the meeting enter *9 on the phone’s key pad to
activate the “raise hand” button at the time the Agenda Item is being presented for City Council
consideration.

PRESENTATIONS Southern California Edison Compliance Advisor, Traci Degnan, will provide

the state mandated Annual Propane Gas Safety Public Awareness presentation.

CONSENT CALENDAR

1.  Minutes
  Although the live recording is the official record of public meetings, actions are prepared
  for the Council’s approval.
  Recommended Action
  Approve minutes from the November 28, 2023 regular City Council Meeting.

2.  Warrants
  Expenditures Submitted for Approval
  o Warrants in the amount of $719,170.84.
  o Warrant from the CIMC Improvement Fund totaling $119,712.96.
  o One payroll totaling $233,097.90.
  o Three electronic fund transfers totaling $89,859.50.
  Recommended Action
  Approve total expenditures for November 20, 2023 through December 1, 2023 totaling
  $1,161,841.20.

3.  Development Impact Fees Annual Report for the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 2023
  In February 2020, City Council adopted the findings of the development impact fee nexus
  study and established certain development impact fees and capacity charges. Reporting
  requirements under California Government Code 66006 specify that the City must
  prepare annual reports of Development Impact Fees within 180 days of the close of the
  fiscal year.
  Recommended Action
  Receive and file the Fiscal Year 2022-23 Development Impact Fees Annual Report.
 CITY COUNCILIHOUSING AUTHORITYISUCCESSOR AGENCY AGENDA
DECEMBER 12, 2023
PAGE 3
**
  The following item on the Consent Calendar is the City Council acting as the Housing
Authority **

4.  Housing Successor Agency Annual Report for Fiscal Year 2022-23
  Health and Safety Code Section 34176.1 requires successor housing entities to prepare
  an annual report documenting compliance with expenditure proportionality and other
  requirements pertaining to the housing asset fund. The report is due to the California
  Department of Housing and Community Development by December 31, 2023.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution approving a Housing Authority Successor Agency Annual Report for
  Fiscal Year 2022-23.
**
 The following item on the Consent Calendar is the City Council acting as the Successor
Agency to the Avalon Community Improvement Agency **

 5.  Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule (ROPS) 24-25 and Successor Agency
  Administrative Budget for Fiscal Year 2024-25
  As a result of the dissolution of redevelopment, the Successor Agency was created to
  administer the enforceable obligations and unwind the affairs of the former Avalon
  Community Improvement Agency. As part of that process, the Successor Agency must
  annually adopt the Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule, as required by Dissolution
  Law.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt ‘A Resolution of the Successor Agency to the Avalon Community Improvement
  Agency Approving a Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule 24-25 and Successor
  Agency Administrative Budget for Fiscal Year 2024-25.’

GENERAL BUSINESS

6.  Cruise Ship Annual Report for the year ending December 31, 2023
  In December 2022, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 22-55 establishing guidelines
  for the approval of cruise ships visiting Avalon through December 31, 2024. The
  guidelines re-affirmed the framework by which cruise ships would be approved to visit
  Avalon as a port of call.
  Recommended Action
  Receive and file the Cruise Ship Annual Report for the calendar year ending December
  31, 2023.

7.  Authorization to Procure Various Process Analyzers for WWTP.
  PERC Water maintains the City’s WWTP, and is requesting to procure various process
  analyzing equipment for the plant from Hach Company. The efficient and reliable
  operation of the treatment plant is essential to ensuring the environmental health and
  safety of our community. The proposed equipment includes chlorine probes & controllers,
 CITY COUNCIL/HOUSING AUTHORITY/SUCCESSOR AGENCY AGENDA
DECEMBER 12, 2023
PAGE 4

  dissolved oxygen (DO.) probes & controllers, and turbidity probes & controllers.
  Recommended Action
  (1) Make the affirmative finding that the Hach Company has satisfied the sole source
  requirement as specified in the Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.111(b). (2)
  Authorize PERC Water to procure various process analyzing equipment from Hach
  Company for the Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP) (3) Allocate funds from Sewer
  Fund 108-25-6552 for the procurement in the amount of not to exceed $89,900.

S.  First Reading of an Ordinance Amending Title 2. Chapter 2-2, Section 2-2.307 City
  Manager Powers and Duties of the Avalon Municipal Code
  City Staff recommend amending Title 2, Chapter 2-2, Section 2-2.307 of the Avalon
  Municipal Code to broaden the powers of the City Manager to include appointment,
  removal, promotion and demotion of the office of the City Clerk.
  Recommended Action
  Introduce and waive the all further readings of an ordinance of the City of Avalon
  amending Title 2, Chapter 2-2, Section 2-2.307 City Manager Powers and Duties of the
  Avalon Municipal Code.

9.  Award Above Ground Fuel Tank Installation and Site Remediation Contract
  The State of California requires the owners or operators of specific types of underground
  fuel storage tanks to permanently close by December 31, 2025. The City of Avalon owns
  four underground fuel tanks at the Avalon Fuel Dock that fall under this requirement. A
  REP for the third and final procurement component of this project above ground fuel
  —

  tank installation, removal of existing underground storage tanks, and site remediation  —

  will close on December 11, 2023 at 3:00 p.m.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to negotiate and execute the contract for the above ground
  fuel tank installation and site remediation project to the lowest, responsible bidder.

10.  Solicitation of Request for Qualified Bidders for Phase II of the Cabrillo Mole Fern’
  Terminal Rehabilitation Project
  The Cabrillo Mote Ferry Terminal is a multimodal transportation hub used by cross-
  channel carrier passengers traveling between the City and the mainland, cruise ship
  disembarkment/embarkment, and serves as the primary entry point to the City. The
  second phase of the project will replace and reconfigure the existing structures to improve
  passenger queuing and adjacent transportation circulation. City Staff has determined the
  best and most efficient way to move the project forward is through a design-build process.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager, or his designee, to solicit a request for qualifications to
  determined appropriate bidders for a design-build contractor for Phase II of the Cabrillo
  Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project.

   AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 28, 2023
  THIS VIRTUAL MEETING IS HELD PURSUANT TO AB 361
  MINUTES

Due to social distancing recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State
of California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA) and the County of
Los Angeles, and pursuant to findings made under AR 361, the CITY OF AVALON’S CITY
COUNCIL SHALL GENERALLY BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC REMOTELY. The
general public may attend the meeting in the Council Chambers however must adhere to
social distancing requirements. The public is encouraged to watch and participate from
the safety of their homes while practicing social distancing.

Council Chambers are open to the general public. Once the Council Chambers reach
maximum occupancy (as determined by the Fire Chief), the general public may participate
in Oral Communication and address the City Council on an agenda item in person by
waiting in the City Hall Court Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time at the
appropriate time. No one will be admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or exhibiting
symptoms of COVID-19. Additionally, the general public may participate in Oral
Communication and address the City Council on an agenda items by providing comments
via Zoom or by sending comments to ask@.cityofavalon.com.

CALL TO ORDER: 5:00 p.m.

Councilmembers Lisa Lavelle, Michael Ponce, Mary Schickling and Yesenia De La Rosa.
Also present: City Manager David Maistros, City Attorney Scott Campbell and Deputy City
Clerk Gabrielle Morones.

10.  Revised Fiscal Year 2023-2024 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule
  (1.) Heard a presentation regarding the Miscellaneous Fee Schedule. (2.) Mayor
  Marshall opened the Public Hearing, no comments were made. (3.) Mayor
  Marshall closed the Public Hearing. (4.) Consensus was made to adopt the fee
  schedule with revisions as proposed and adopted Resolution No. 23-45 of the City
  Council of the City of Avalon Sefting Fees for Services, Facilities and Activities of
  the City of Avalon for Fiscal Year 2023-24.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Michael Ponce. (All Ayes)

11.  Public Hearing Appeal of the Decision of the Vehicle Hearing Officer: Denial of
  —

  a Renewal for a Commercial Autoette Permit
  (1.) Mayor Marshall open the Public Hearing. (2.) Public Comments were heard
  from the applicant Shawn Cape of Dive Catalina, Lily Chu and Fire Chief Michael
  Alegria. (3.) Mayor Marshall closed the Public Hearing. (4.) City Council considered
  applicants appeal and determined to a). Uphold the decision of the Vehicle
  Hearing Officer’s findings and decision dated September 6, 2023.

  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Lisa Lavelle. (4 Ayes
  Marshall, De La Rosa, Lavelle and Ponce; 1 No-Schickling).

  Shawn Cape of Dive Catalina requested that the appeal fee of $455 be waived.
  Motion to approve made by Anni Marshall, seconded by Michael Ponce.
  (All Ayes)

GENERAL BUSINESS

12.  Authorization to Purchase Spare Pump for Catherine Lift Station
  (1.) Made the affirmative finding that the Xylem, Inc. has satisfied the sole
  source requirement as specified in the Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-
  4.111(b). (2.) Authorized the purchase of a Flygt 6” submersible sewage pump
  from Xylem, Inc. to be placed in inventory and be available for immediate
  replacement for a not-to-exceed cost of $28,500. (3.) Allocated funds from
  Sewer Fund 108-25-6552 for the procurement in the amount of not-to-exceed
  $28,500.
  Motion to approve made by Anni, seconded by Michael Ponce. (All Ayes)

13.  Approval of Encroachment Permit for a Grease Interceptor within Third Street
  Adiacent to the Lobster Trap Restaurant
  (1.) Approved an encroachment permit for a 750-gallon grease interceptor within
  Third Street adjacent to 126 Catalina Avenue, the Lobster Trap restaurant; and
  (2.) Authorized the City Manager to negotiate with the property owner to
 CITY COUNCIL MINUTES
NOVEMBER 28, 2023
PAGE 4

  determine the precise location of the installation, and the amounts of the required
  bond and liability insurance.
  (3.) Adopted Resolution No. 23-46 of the City Council of the City of Avalon
  Approving an Encroachment Permit to Allow Installation of a 750-Gallon Grease
  Interceptor within the Public Right-of-Way Along Third Street.

  Michael Ponce recused himself due to a Conflict of Interest.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Yesenia De La Rosa.
  (4 Ayes-Marshall1 De La Rosa, Lavelle and Schickling; 1 Abstention-Ponce).

14.  Authorization to Upgrade Communication Equipment at WWTP
  (1.) Authorized PERC Water to have The LeMasters Company (TLC) replace the
  existing communication equipment for the Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP)
  with the radio based Phoenix System. (2.) Allocated funds from Sewer Fund 108-
  25-6552 for the procurement in the amount of not-to-exceed $110,522.50.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Anni Marshall.
  (All Ayes).

15.  Annual Love Catalina Tourism Authority Report
  Received and filed report.

CLOSED SESSION-7:21 p.m.-7:59 p.m.

Following the appropriate announcement of the Closed Session items the City Council
went into Closed Session to discuss the following:

  1. CONFERENCE WITH LEGAL COUNSEL INITIATION OF LITIGATION
  —

  Initiation of litigation pursuant to 54956.9(c):
  One (1) case.

  2. PUBLIC EMPLOYEE APPOINTMENT
  Title: City Clerk

Following Closed Session the Mayor announced there was no reportable action.

Mayor Marshall adjourned the meeting at 7:59 p.m.

I, Gabrielle Morones, Deputy City Clerk, do hereby certify that the DVD videotape of the
Regular City Council Meeting on November 28, 2023, is the official record of the Council
Meeting and is on file and maintained in City Hall.

SUBJECT:  Development Impact Fees Annual Report for the Fiscal Year Ended
  June 30, 2023

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Receive and file the Fiscal Year 2022-23 Development Impact
Fees Annual Report.

REPORT SUMMARY: On February 18, 2020, City Council adopted the findings of the
development impact fee nexus study and established certain development impact fees and
capacity charges. Development impact fees (DIEs) are fees charged by a local government
agency that developers and applicants pay for either all or a portion of the cost of providing
public infrastructure and services to the new development. DIFs can also help streamline the
development approval process as the typical impacts will have been identified and quantified in
a per unit basis, in advance of any development proposal. Capacity charges are City imposed
charges on new development for existing and/or future wastewater capacity needed for new
development.

Reporting requirements under California Government Code 66006 specify that the City must
prepare annual reports of Development Impact Fees within 180 days of the close of the fiscal
year. The fiscal year ended June 30, 2023 was the third year with fees paid subject to
reporting requirements. The report describes the fees: the amount of the fees collected,
interest earned, and identification of any expenditures from those funds. The FY 2022-23
Development Impact Fee Annual Report is attached for City Council’s review and approval.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Compliance with reporting requirements

FISCAL IMPACTS: There is no fiscal impact by the recommended action as this reports
development impact fee activity for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: N/A

FOLLOW UP ACTION: N/A

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: Pursuant to the Brown Act.

 Legal Requirements for Development Impact Fee Reporting

California Government Code Section 66006 (b)

California Government Code Section 66006 (b) defines the specific reporting requirements for
local agencies that impose AB 1600 DIFs on new development. Annually, for each separate fund
established for the collection and expenditure of DIFs, the local agency shall, within 180 days of
the close of the fiscal year, make available to the public the information shown below for the most
recent fiscal year.

  a) A brief description of the type of fee in the account or fund.
  b) The amount of the fee.
  c) The beginning and ending balance of the account or fund.
  d) The amount of the fees collected and interest earned.
  e) An identification of each public improvement on which fees were expended and the amount
  of the expenditures on each improvement, including the total percentage of the cost of the
  public improvement that was funded with fees.
  f) An identification of an approximate date by which the construction of the public
  improvement will commence if the local agency determines that sufficient hinds have been
  collected to complete financing on an incomplete public improvement, as identified in
  paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 66001, and the public improvement remains
  incomplete.
  g) A description of each inter-fund transfer or loan made from the account or fund, including
  the public improvement on which the transferred or loaned fees will be expended, and, in
  the case of an inter-hind loan, the date on which the loan will be repaid, and the rate of
  interest that the account or fund will receive on the loan.
  h) The amount of refunds made pursuant to subdivision (e) of Section 66001 and any
  allocations pursuant to subdivision (1) of Section 66001.

California Govermnent Code Section 66001 (d)

For all funds established for the collection and expenditure of DIFs. California Government Code
Section 66001 (d) has additional requirements. For the fifth fiscal year following the first deposit
into the fund and every five years thereafter, the local agency shall make all of the following
findings with respect to that portion of the fund remaining unexpended, whether committed or
u nco in ni it ted:

  a) Identify the purpose to which the fee is to be put.
  b) Demonstrate a reasonable reLationship between the fee and purpose for which it is charged.
  c) Identify all sources and amounts of funding anticipated to complete financing in
  incomplete improvements identified in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a).

California Government Code Section 66002

The State of California Government Code Section 66002 states that:

  a) Any local agency, which levies a fee subject to Section 66001, may adopt a capital
  improvement plan, which shall indicate the approximate location, size, time of availability,
  and estimates of cost for all facilities or improvements to be financed with the fees.

  h) The capital improvement plan shall be adopted by, and shall he annually updated by, a
  resolution of the governing body of the local agency adopted at a noticed public hearing.
  Notice of the hearing shall be given pursuant to Section 65090. In addition, mailed notice
  shall be given to any city or county. which may be significantly affected by the capital
  improvement plan. This notice shalL be given no later than the date the local agency notices
  the public hearing pursuant to Section 65090. The information in the notice shall be not
  less than the infonnation contained in the notice of public hearing and shall be given by
  first-class mail or personaL delivery.

  c)  ‘Facility” or “improvement.” as used in this section. means any of the following:

  I) Public buildings, including schools and related facilities; provided that school
  facilities shall not be included if Senate Bill 97 of the 1987-88 Regular Session is
  enacted and becomes effective on or before January 1, 1988.
  2) Facilities for the storage. treatment. and distribution of nonagricultural water.
  3) Facilities for the collection, treatment. reclamation, and disposal of sewage.
  4) Facilities for the collection and disposal of storm waters and for flood control
  purposes.
  5) Facilities for the generation of electricity and the distribution of gas and electricity.
  6) Transportation and transit facilities, including but not limited to streets and
  supporting improvements, roads. overpasses, bridges, harbors, ports, airports, and
  related facilities.
  7) Parks and recreation facilities.
  8) Any other capital project identified in the capital facilities plan adopted pursuant to
  Section 66002.

REPORT SUMMARY:
Housing Successor Agency Annual Report
Health and Safety Code Section 34176.1 (enacted by Senate Bill 341 and Assembly Bill 1793)
requires successor housing entities to prepare an annual report documenting compliance with
expenditure proportionality and other requirements pertaining to the housing asset fund. The
report is due to the California Department of Housing and Community Development by
December 31, 2023.

The Annual Report includes the following information required by law:
  • Amounts deposited into the Housing Asset Fund;
  • Statement of the balance of the Housing Asset Fund;
  • Description of expenditures by category;
  • Statutory value of real property;
  • Description of transfers from the former Avalon Community Improvement Agency;
  • Description of projects that receive funding through the Successor Agency’s
  Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule;
  Status of property disposition efforts;
  Update on inclusionary and replacement housing obligations;
  Compliance with five-year expenditure obligations;
  Percentage of senior deed-restricted units;
  Amount of excess surplus; and
  An inventory of homeownership units with affordability restrictions.

Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund
The Housing Asset Fund includes all of the assets that were transferred from the Avalon
Community Improvement Agency (“AdA”) to the Housing Authority upon dissolution of the
ACIA. The assets include:

  •  Real properties,
  •  Affordable housing covenants,
  •  Loan receivables,
  Page 1 of 3
   •  Income from ground leases and rental properties, and
  •  Supplemental Educational Revenue Augmentation Fund Loan.

A total of $11013 was deposited into the Housing Asset Fund during the fiscal year. At the
close of Fiscal Year 2022-23, the ending asset balance in the Housing Asset Fund was
$5,541,154. Land held for resale and cash constitute most this amount. The Housing Asset
Fund had a cash balance of approximately $1 ,592244 at the close of the fiscal year.

There were no expenditures from the Housing Asset Fund in Fiscal Year 2022-23. The
statutory value of the properties and loans transferred to the Housing Authority totals
$4,371,426.

Property and Project Descriptions
The ACIA transferred seven real properties to the Housing Authority that were approved by
DOF in 2012. The Housing Authority sold two of the properties in FY 2013-14, with the
following five properties remaining:

  •  309 Beacon Street
  •  313 Beacon Street
  •  238 Descanso Avenue
  •  311 DescansoAvenue
  •  206 E. Whittley Avenue

All of the properties with the exception of 206 E. Whittley Avenue have been developed for
affordable housing purposes and are in compliance with property disposition requirements. A
multi-family property at 206 E. Whittley Avenue was purchased by the ACIA in 2008 with the
intent to develop new affordable housing units. However, the ACIA was unable to pursue
development due to the dissolution of redevelopment. In July 2019, the City Council acting as
Housing Authority approved the final construction plans and authorized staff to develop and
release the request for proposals to rehabilitate the property to be rented to low and moderate
income residents and in October 2019, authorized City Staff to move forward in developing a
preliminary site plan and feasibility study for the development of five units, through the
replacement of one unit and addition of four new units. The Authority undertook site work
activity in FY 2022-23, and construction is anticipated to commence in the upcoming fiscal
year.

Outstanding lncIusionay and Replacement Housing Obligations
The former ACIA had a 52-unit surplus of affordable housing units as of February 1, 2012.
Therefore, there are no outstanding affordable unit production obligations to fulfill.

Income & Age Proportionality
If housing successors expend money on projects, SB 341 requires at least 30 percent to be
spent on extremely law-income rental housing, among other restrictions. The Housing
Authority has only expended funds on administrative costs since becoming the housing
successor. As such, the Housing Authority is in compliance with expenditure proportionality
requirements.

  Page 2 of 3
 SB 341 also sets a limit on the portion of publicly assisted deed-restricted rental housing that
may be restricted to seniors. There have been no deed-restricted rental units assisted by the
Housing Authority or City in the past 10 years, therefore the Housing Authority is in compliance
with this requirement.

Excess Surplus
SB 341 reinstated a requirement to prevent housing successors from accumulating an excess
surplus, which is generally defined as unencumbered cash that exceeds the greater of $1
million or the aggregate amount deposited into the Housing Asset Fund in the preceding four
years. Since the housing successor did not exist until 2012, the first year this calculation can
be performed is Fiscal Year 2016-17. The Housing Authority previously accumulated an
excess surplus in FY 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22 totaling $517,338. The Housing Authority
encumbered the excess surplus to the 206 E. Whittley Avenue housing development within
three fiscal years, as required, and did not have an excess surplus in FY 2022-23.

Homeownership UnIt Inventory
The Housing Authority oversees five homeownership units with affordability restrictions. All
units are moderate-income households assisted through the First-Time Homebuyer Program.

 INTRODUCTION

The Avaton Housing Authority (Housing Authority’) is the Housing Successor Agency to the former
Avalon Community Improvement Agency (“ACIA”). The Rousing Authority is responsible for maintaining
housing assets transferred from the former AdA, and its main goal is to provide affordable housing for
Avalon residents.

This Housing Successor Agency Annual Report (Annual Report”) contains information on Fiscal Year
(“FY”) 2022-23 finances and activities as required by Health and Safety Code (‘HSC”) Section 34176.1 (f).

This Annual Report details how the Housing Authority met all requirements for expenditures by income
level since the beginning of the second five-year compliance period, which runs from July 1, 2019 through
June 30. 2024.

The Annual Report is due to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (“HCD”)
by December 31 annually and must be accompanied by an independent financial audit. The Housing
Authority’s audited financial statements will be posted on the City of Avalon’s (“City”) website when
available.1 This report is an addendum to the Housing Authority Annual Report required by HSC Section
34328, which is submitted to HCD by October V annually.

HOUSING SUCCESSOR REQUIREMENTS  -—

In the 2013-14 Legislative Session, Senate Bill (“SB”) 341 and subsequent legislation enacted several
requirements for housing successor agencies. Housing successors must comply with three major
requirements pursuant to HSC Section 34176.1:

  1.  Expenditures and housing production are subject to income and age targets.

  2.  Housing successors may not accumulate an “excess surplus,” or a high balance based on certain
  thresholds discussed later in this report.

   3.  Properties must be developed with affordable housing within five to ten years of being approved
  for transfer from the former redevelopment agency to the housing successor.

The requirements are designed to ensure that housing successors are actively utilizing former ACIA
housing assets to produce affordable housing. Appendix 1 provides a detailed summary of the reporting
requirements that are addressed in this Annual Report.

ASSETS TRANSFERRED TO HOUSING SUCCESSOR
Upon the statewide dissolution of redevelopment in 2012, all rights, powers, committed assets, liabilities,
duties, and obligations associated with the housing activities of the ACIA were transferred to the Housing
Authority. The Housing Authority prepared a Housing Asset Transfer Form (HAT’) that provided an
inventory of all housing assets transferred from the ACIA to the Housing Authority. This included:

  1. Real properties,

  2. Affordable housing covenants,

  3. Loan receivables,

  4.  Income from ground leases and rental properties, and

  5.  Supplemental Educational Revenue Augmentation Fund (“SERAF”) Loan.

All items on HAT were approved by the California Department of Finance (‘DOF”) on August 30, 2012.
DOF later asked the Successor Agency to revise the form, and the revised HAT was approved by DOF
on December 15, 2014. A copy of the revised HAT is provided as Appendix 2.

It is important to distinguish that Housing Authority assets that were not transferred from the former AdA.
nor generated by, nor purchased with, assets from the former ACIA, are not subject to HSC Section
34176.1.

 HOUSING ASSET FUND ACTIVITY

Former ACIA assets, and the revenues generated by those assets, are maintained in a Low and Moderate
Income Housing Asset Fund (‘Housing Asset Fund”).2 Housing Asset Funds may be spent on:

  •  Administrative costs for operation of the housing successor agency. The law allows a housing
  successor to spend the greater of:

  o  $200,000 per year adjusted for inflation, or

  o  5% of the statutory value of real property owned by that housing successor and the value
  of loans and grants receivable from the HAT (“Portfolio”).

  According to HCD, the $200,000 hmit adjusted for inflation is $254,500 for FY 2022-23. The
  Housing Successor will comply with the FY 2022-23 limit since administrative expenses were
  below $254,500.

  •  Homeless prevention and rapid rehousing services up to $250,000 per year if the formerAClA
  did not have any outstanding housing inclusionary or replacement housing production
  requirements. The former ACIA had a surplus of affordable housing production units, and
  therefore the Housing Authority as Housing Successor can make this expenditure if it chooses
  and funding is available for such expenditures.

  •  Affordable housing development assisting households up to 80 percent of the Area Median
  Income (‘AMI”), subject to specific income and age targets.

  Five-Year Income Proportionality; If any Housing Asset Funds are spent on affordable
  housing development, it triggers a requirement to spend at least 30 percent of such expenses
  assisting extremely low-income households (30% AMI). and no more than 20 percent on low-

BACKGROUND

As a result of the dissolution of redevelopment, the Successor Agency was created to
administer the enforceable obligations and unwind the affairs of the former Avalon Community
Improvement Agency (‘Former Agency”). As part of that process, the Successor Agency must
annually adopt the Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule (“ROPS”), as required by
Dissolution Law.

AVALON ROPS 24-25
A Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule for the 2024-25 fiscal period (“ROPS 24-25”),
covering the period of July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025, is required to be submitted to the State
Department of Finance (“DOE’) by February 1, 2024. If the ROPS is not submitted by that
deadline, the City of Avalon (as the City and not as the Successor Agency) will be subject to a
civil penalty of $10,000 per day for each day it is late.
DOF provided the Successor Agency with a partially completed ROPS form to standardize the
form and make it consistent with the automated tracking system. Commencing October 1,
2018 and annually thereafter, the differences between actual payments and past estimated
and approved obligations on the ROPS shall be submitted by the Successor Agency to the Los
Angeles County Auditor-Controller for review and adjustment to future distributions through a
Prior Period Adjustment (“PPA”) form. The County Auditor-Controller has until February 1 to
submit the reviewed PPA to DOE for DOE approval.
A PPA form for ROPS 21-22 was submitted by Avalon Successor Agency staff to the County
Auditor-Controller before the October 1, 2023 deadline. Because the ROPS is an estimate of
the funds needed to pay enforceable obligations, often times the requested amounts vary from
the actual expenditure. During the ROPS 21-22 period1 the PPA showed that the Avalon
Successor Agency spent $1,850 less Redevelopment Property Tax Rust Funds (“RPTTF”)

  Page 1 of 4
 than requested on fiscal agent fees. The unspent $1850 will likely be deducted from the Fiscal
Year 2024-25 RPTTF distribution.

  •  Debt service payments on the 2003 Tax Allocation Bonds, Series A;

  and 20158;

SUCCESSOR AGENCY ADMINISTRATIVE BUDGET (FISCAL YEAR 24-25)
California Health and Safety Code (“HSC”) Section 34177(j) requires the Successor Agency to
prepare an Administrative Budget and submit it to the Oversight Board for approval. Pursuant
to HSC Section 34171 (b), the administrative allowance is limited to the greater of $250,000
per year, or three percent (3%) of the RPTTF distributed in the prior fiscal year, excluding the
administrative allowance and any City/Former Agency loan repayments.

Staff has completed a projection funding needed for the 2024-25 fiscal year and is
recommending that the Successor Agency approve an annual administrative budget of
$150,000, which is split evenly between the two six-month ROPS periods, and direct staff to
submit the budget to the Oversight Board for approval. Administrative activities for the 2024-25
fiscal year include preparation and legal review of the ROPS, PPA, staff reports and
resolutions, payment of enforceable obligations, affendance at Successor Agency and

LAST AND FINAL ROPS
Beginning January 1, 2016, successor agencies may submit a Last and Final ROPS for
approval by the oversight board and DOE if all of the following conditions are met:

  1. Remaining debt includes only administrative costs and enforceable obligations with set
  payment schedules, such as debt service, loan agreements, and contracts;
  2. All remaining obligations have been previously listed on a ROPS and approved by DOF;
  and
  3. The successor agency has no outstanding or unresolved litigation.
The Successor Agency meets these conditions but we do not believe that now is the time to
submit a Last and Final ROPS. Once DOE approves a successor agency’s Last and Final
ROPS, the successor agency may submit up to two requests to amend it.
A consideration with a Last and Final ROPS is the likelihood of the recurring administrative
cost allowance being significantly reduced. DOE has indicated that the administrative cost
allowance on a Last and Final ROPS should be expected to be reduced to approximately
$5,000 per approved line item per year as a general rule of thumb. This is similar to what other
Successor Agencies who have filed a Last and Final ROPS have had their administrative cost
allowance reduced to.
Avalon will need to weigh the fiscal consequences on the City General Fund, with a potential
loss of the recurring administrative cost allowances. Ultimately, the taxing agencies, including
the City, share in the benefits of a Last and Final ROPS over the short term, but long term the
City may be at risk of losing the greater administrative cost allowance. Every successor
agency faces this issue; however, ultimately the administrative cost allowance will end once
enforceable obligations are retired. Successor Agency staff and the Successor Agency’s
financial consultant, RSG, Inc., will continue to analyze the potential impacts of submitting a
Last and Final ROPS.
OVERSIGHT BOARD CONSOLIDATION
Oversight boards have broad authority to set administrative budgets, approve the transfer of
properties pursuant to a long-range property management plan, approve enforceable
obligations, and otherwise direct the successor agency to perform activities to wind down the
former redevelopment agencies.
The Dissolution Act (specifically HSC Section 34179(j-q)) provides that local oversight boards
are succeeded by a single Countywide oversight board (with the exception of Los Angeles
County, where 5 oversight boards have been created), commencing on July 1, 2016. The
ROPS and Administrative Budget prepared by the Successor Agency for FY 2024-25 will be
reviewed by the District 4 Los Angeles County Oversight Board.

SUBJECT:  Cruise Ship Annual Report for the year ending December 31, 2023

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Receive and file the Cruise Ship Annual Report for the
calendar year ending December 31, 2023

REPORT SUMMARY: On December 22, 2022, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 22-
55 establishing guidelines for the approval of cruise ships visiting Avalon through December
31, 2024. The guidelines re-affirmed the framework by which cruise ships would be approved
to visit Avalon as a port of call. Guidelines include:

  1. Number of regularly scheduled cruise ship vessels shall not exceed 3 per week during
  the Summer Season (Memorial Day to Labor Day) without final written approval of the
  City Manager.

  2. No cruise ship vessels shall be allowed on the weekends during the Summer Season or
  during special event weekends without final written approval of the City Manager.

  3. Number of regularly scheduled cruise ship vessels shall not exceed 3 per week during
  the ‘off season” (Labor Day to Memorial Day) without final written approval of the City
  Manager.

  4. Repositioning, infrequent, or small cruise ship vessels (1000 passengers or less) may
  be considered for visitation by the Harbor Master, taking into account the day
  requested, holidays, events, harbor activities, impacts to public safety, etc.

The resolution further requires the Harbor Master and Finance Director to provide an annual
report on cruise ship vessels that includes the number of vessels that visit Avalon, number of
passengers, amount of wharfage collected, any safety or security incidents that may have
occurred while the ship was in port, as well as projections and scheduling information for the
next year.

SUBJECT:  Authorization to procure various process analyzers for WWTP.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): (1) Make the affirmative finding that the Hach Company has
satisfied the sole source requirement as specified in the Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-
4.111(b). (2) Authorize PERC Water to procure various process analyzing equipment from Hach
Company for the Wastewater Treatment Plant (VWVTP) (3) Allocate funds from Sewer Fund 108-
25-6552 for the procurement in the amount of not to exceed S89,900.

REPORT SUMMARY: PERC Water maintains the City’s WWFP, and is requesting to procure
various process analyzing equipment for the plant from Hach Company. The efficient and
reliable operation of the treatment plant is essential to ensuring the environmental health and
safety of our community. The proposed equipment includes chlorine probes & controllers,
dissolved oxygen (D.C.) probes & controllers, and turbidity probes & controllers.
The wastewater treatment plant plays a crucial role in treating and purifying the city’s
wastewater before it is released back into the environment. To maintain the plant’s
effectiveness, it is imperative to invest in state-of-the-art process analyzers. These analyzers
will provide real-time data and control capabilities for key parameters, ensuring optimal plant
performance. Hach Company will also be providing a service agreement, installation, training
and a warranty covering all equipment. The scope of equipment is as follows.
  1. Chlorine Probes and Controllers:
  •  Chlorine monitoring is essential for disinfection purposes in wastewater
  treatment.
  •  The proposed probes and controllers will enable accurate and continuous
  monitoring of chlorine levels, allowing for timely adjustments to ensure
  compliance with environmental regulations.
  2. Dissolved Oxygen (D.O.) Probes and Controllers:
  •  Monitoring dissolved oxygen levels is critical for the biological treatment
  processes in the plant.
  •  The D.C. probes and controllers will provide precise measurements, allowing for
  the adjustment of aeration rates to optimize biological treatment efficiency.
   3. Turbidity Probes and Controllers:
  •  Turbidity is a key indicator of water clarity and the effectiveness of the treatment
  processes.
  •  The proposed turbidity probes and controllers will enable real-time monitoring,
  facilitating prompt responses to any deviations in water clarity and ensuring the
  quality of the treated effluent.
Real-time data from the analyzers will enable proactive adjustments, leading to improved
treatment efficiency and reduced operational costs, Accurate monitoring of key parameters
ensures that the wastewater treatment plant consistently meets and exceeds environmental
regulations. By investing in advanced analyzers, we contribute to minimizing the environmental
impact of our wastewater discharge, promoting sustainability.
Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Section 3-4.106 (b) requires purchases of goods, services,
supplies and equipment with a value over S25,000 be a publically noticed low bid procurement.
However, AMC Section 3-41 11(b) allows the City to dispense with bidding if there is only one
source for the procurement (sole source) or when the City makes the determination that the
purchase can be made more economically and/or efficiently without bidding procedures. In this
case, Hach Company is the exclusive supplier of the proposed equipment in our region. It is
recommended that the City Council approve the procurement of the analyzing equipment from
Hach Company for the WWtP and authorize the allocation of funds for the project from the
Emergency Repair Sewer Fund a cost not to exceed $89,900. Additional funds were included
to account for tax & shipping of the equipment.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Infrastructure reliability and safety.

FISCAL IMPACTS: A cost not to exceed of $89900. Sufficient funds exist in FY 23-24 Sewer
Fund 108-25-6552.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: PERC Water will not
have the proper equipment to effectively monitor wastewater data which could create
compliance issues with the State Water Board leading to potential violations and fines.

SUBJECT:  First Reading of an Ordinance Amending Title 2, Chapter 2-2,
  Section 2-2.307 City Manager Powers and Duties of the Avalon
  Municipal Code

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Introduce and waive the all further readings of an ordinance of
the City of Avalon amending Title 2, Chapter 2-2, Section 2-2.307 City Manager Powers and
Duties of the Avalon Municipal Code.

REPORT SUMMARY: City Staff recommend amending Title 2, Chapter 2-2, Section 2-2.307 of
the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) to broaden the powers of the City Manager to include
appointment, removal, promotion and demotion of the office of the City Clerk.

As written, the AMC exempts the office of the City Clerk as the position is appointed by resolution
of the City Council. City Staff recommend reorganizing the structure of the office of the City Clerk
to have the office report directly to the City Manager rather than the City Council. With this
proposed amendment the City Manager will provide oversight of the City Clerk’s Office.

The office of the City Clerk is administrative in nature with the City Clerk providing oversight of
public records requests, compliance with various governmental regulations, including annual
reporting to the FPPC and citywide records management. The City Clerk also acts as the local
elections official.

In recent history, the City Clerk position has been a dual title held in conjunction with the City
Manager or Chief Administrative Officer. At this time, the City does not have a permanent and
dedicated City Clerk. Duties of the City Clerk Office are shared divided between a Deputy City
Clerk/Senior Administrative Assistant and Management Analyst.

Additionally, Staff are taking this opportunity to further amend the ordinance to make it gender
neutral when referencing the City Manager.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The Avalon Municipal
Code will not be amended.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Adoption of the Ordinance at the next regular City Council meeting.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: This item was properly listed on the posted
agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

2-2.307 City Manager Powers and Duties.

SUBJECT:  Award Above Ground Fuel Tank Installation and Site Remediation
  Contract

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to negotiate and execute the
contract for the above ground fuel tank installation and site remediation project to the lowest,
responsible bidder.

REPORT SUMMARY: The State of California requires the owners or operators of specific types
of underground fuel storage tanks to permanently close by December 31, 2025. The City of
Avalon owns four underground fuel tanks at the Avalon Fuel Dock that fall under this
requirement.

With assistance from former Assemblymember Patrick O’Donnell, the City was awarded a
$500,000 State budget earmark that is administered through the State of California Water Board
to remove the underground fuel tanks located at the fuel dock and install an above ground
system in compliance with the new regulations. The granting agreement requires the City to
have construction completed and the project closed out by June 30, 2024.

The project is included in the FY22-23 Budget and Capital Improvement Plan  —  Project Number
207004, Account Number 11470-6547 with S700,000 budgeted.
  —

On March 21, 2023 City Council approved the design and construction documents for this
project, and authorized Staff to post and receive informal bids to procure the fuel tank for an
amount not to exceed $200,000. On June 27, 2023, the City Council awarded a contract to
Western Pump fora not-to-exceed amount of $160,000.

As the second component of this project, on August 11, 2023 the City solicited bids by informal
bid process from duly licensed and experienced contractors to provide site preparation, grading,
concrete foundation, retaining wall installation and related construction services for the new
location of the storage tank. After an extension of the bid deadline, bidding closed on August 28,
2023 at 1 pm. Only Jordahl Construction, Inc provided a bid of $274,710 by the stated deadline.
On September 5, 2023 the City Council determined the contract cost was reasonable and
awarded the contract to Jordahl Construction by adopting Resolution 23-35 by a 4/5 vote.
 On December 1, 2023, City Staff solicited a RFP for the third and final procurement component
of this project above ground fuel tank installation, removal of existing underground storage
  —

tanks, and site remediation. The REP for this scope of work closes on December 11, 2023 at
3:00 pm., the day before the City Council meeting. At the time this report was authored, 13
firms had accessed the REP via the City’s website www.cityotavaloncorn/rfp.
  —

Staff will provide proposals submitted under separate cover, including a cost analysis and other
relevant information.

Time is of the essence as this project must have construction completed and project closed out
by June 30, 2024.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: City Infrastructure. Reduction of high-risk facilities.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Project budgeted in CIP project code 207004 (account 11470-6547).

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City may not meet
the timeline required by the funding agreement with the State of California Water Board.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Execute an agreement.

agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

  10.1  Cost Breakdown.

  A. Lump Sum Work. Contractor shall furnish on forms approved by the City within ten

  supported by such data to substantiate its accuracy as the Engineer may require.
  This schedule of values, unless objected to by the Engineer, shall be used as a basis
  for reviewing the Contractor’s applications for payment. Contractor shall submit the
  schedule of values prior to submitting its first application for payment, and the City
  will not issue any payment until it receives and approves the schedule of values.

  B. Unit Price Work. Where the Contract Documents provide that all or part of the Work
  is to be Unit Price Work, initially the Contract Price will be deemed to include for all
  Unit Price Work an amount equal to the sum of the unit price for each separately
  identified item of Unit Price Work multiplied by the estimated quantity of each item
  as indicated in the Contract. The estimated quantities of items of Unit Price Work
  are not guaranteed and are solely for the purpose of comparison of Bids and
  determining an initial Contract Price. Each unit price will be deemed to include an
  amount considered by Contractor to be adequate to cover Contractor’s overhead
  and or profit for each separately identified item. Unless otherwise specified, payment

  Engineer, based on the price per unit as set forth in the Bid Schedule.

SUBJECT:  Solicitation of Request for Qualified Bidders for Phase II of the
  Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager, or his designee, to solicit a request
for qualifications to determined qualified bidders for a design-build contractor for Phase II of the
Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project.

REPORT SUMMARY: The Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal is a multimodal transportation hub used
by cross-channel carrier passengers traveling between the City and the mainland! cruise ship
disembarkmentlembarkment, and serves as the primary entry point to the City. In 2020, the City
completed the first phase of its rehabilitation  reinforcing the existing concrete members,
  —

replacing the steel grates, and repairing the concrete deck and railing for a total project cost
  —

of $5.10 million.

The second phase of the project, budgeted at 520 million, will replace and reconfigure the
existing structures to improve passenger queuing and adjacent transportation circulation. In
2022, City Staff! working cooperatively with community stakeholders and the design firm Hart
Howerton, developed a Design Intent document. This document has been shared in a number
of town hall style public meetings and is available for review on the City’s website.

City Staff has determined the best and most efficient way to move the project forward is through
a design-build process. Using Hart Howerton’s Design Intent Document as a guide, City Staff
are currently developing a Design-Build request for proposals (REP) for this project. Public
Contract Code section 22164 establishes statutory measures that must be met in order for the
City to engage in a Design-Build type procurement process.

Specifically, the Public Contract Code requires the City to meet the following criteria:
  -  The project cost must be in excess of Si 000,000. ( 22162(a).)
  -  Only projects for the construction of a building or buildings and improvements directly
  related to the construction of a building or buildings and park and recreational facilities
  may be procured using Design-Build under the law. ( 22i6i(g)(i).)
  -  Before commencing the Design-Build procurement process, the City is required to
  develop and adopt a standard organizational conflict-of-interest policy. ( 22162(c).)

After conferring with the City Attorney’s office, it has been determined that Phase II of the Cabrillo
Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project meets the statutory requirements for a Design-Build
 procurement. Per Public Contract Code section 22164 (b) a two-step REQ-RFP process must
be used to ensure prospective Design-Build firms are first prequalified before they are able to
submit a proposal through a formal RFP process.

The Public Contracts Code outlines what must be included in a REQ including:
  -  Identify the basic scope and needs of the Design-Build project, the expected cost, the
  methodology the City will use to evaluate proposals, the procedure for selection of the
  Design-Build entity and any other information the City deems necessary to inform
  interested firms of the opportunity.

  -  Identify factors the City intends to consider in evaluating whether a firm is qualified,
  including technical design and construction expertise, safety record and other non-price
  related factors.

  -  A template request for statement of qualifications that requires the prospective Design-
  Build entities to submit the following information:
  o The firm’s legal entity type (i.e., corporation, LLC, joint venture, etc...);
  o Evidence that the Design-Build team has completed or demonstrated the ability to
  complete projects that are similar in size, scope, or complexity to the City’s project;
  o Evidence that the proposed key personnel have sufficient experience and training
  to competently manage and complete the design and construction of the project;
  o A financial statement that ensures the Design-Build entity has the capacity to
  complete the project;
  o Evidence of the licenses, registration and credentials required to design and
  construct the project including information on the revocation or suspension of any
  such licenses, registration and credentials;
  o Evidence that the Design-Build entity has the capacity to obtain all required
  payment and performance bonds, liability insurance and errors and omissions
  insurance;
  o Information regarding workers’ compensation experience history and a worker
  safety program; a copy of the organizational documents or agreement forming the
  Design-Build entity; evidence of an acceptable safety record.
  o A certification form requiring the Design-Build entity, including its general partners
  or joint venture members, to certify the information it is providing in response to
  the REQ is certified under penalty of perjury.
  o An agreement form whereby the Design-Build entity agrees to commit to the City
  that the entity, if selected, and its subcontractors at every tier will comply with
  applicable federal or state labor requirements.

The above list represents the minimum information the City must require prospective Design
Build entities to submit in response to the REQ in order to be prequalified. The City may include
additional criteria not listed above at its discretion.

City Staff are currently working cooperatively with the City Attorney’s Office to develop a RFQ.
Simultaneously Staff are developing a comprehensive RFP.
